title: Nanda's vanity
hook: the half-brother confesses he was vain and restless until he learned (Theragatha, Nanda)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sona walked until his feet bled, and the Buddha asked him about a lute, a vina. Your line was not too tight. Today, a monk whose song opens with his vanity.

In one sutta, Nanda comes to the Buddha in pressed robes, with ointment around his eyes and a glazed, shining bowl in his hands. He's the Buddha's half-brother, son of the aunt who raised them both. The Buddha looks at him and says, in effect: this isn't fitting for someone who left home out of faith. Go live in the forest, wear robes made of rags, and stop caring about the pleasures of the senses. Later, Nanda made his own song about who he'd been.
screen: `PRESSED ROBES, A SHINING BOWL.` → `THIS ISN'T FITTING.` → `HIS OWN SONG.`

segments.voice: First, the confession. Nanda's verses in the Theragatha are short, and they open without a defense. Through careless attention, he says, I was given to adornment. I was restless and fickle, burning with desire. No excuse about youth or family. Just: I was vain. Second, the way out. Through the skillful means of the Buddha, kinsman of the sun, he says, I practiced properly and pulled my mind out of the pull of becoming. Third, what skillful means meant in his case. The Udana tells the story. Nanda wants to leave the order. He can't stop thinking of a young Sakyan woman who, as he left home, asked him to come back soon. So the Buddha takes him, the story says, to a heaven, and shows him heavenly women more beautiful than anyone he's seen. Nanda admits the woman at home no longer compares. The Buddha promises him such company if he practices, and Nanda practices, for a reward. The other monks find out and call him a hired hand, working for wages. Ashamed, he goes off alone, practices in earnest, and is freed. Then he releases the Buddha from the promise. He no longer wants the prize. Fourth, what his song leaves out: no heaven, no prize, no teasing monks. Only the plain admission and the plain gratitude. The story is strange and vivid. The song is spare. A man who once dressed for an audience sings verses with nothing dressed up.
screen: `I WAS GIVEN TO ADORNMENT.` · `THROUGH SKILLFUL MEANS.` · `A HIRED HAND, WORKING FOR WAGES.` · `THE SONG LEAVES THE PRIZE OUT.` · then, large: `I WAS VAIN.`

segments.voice: Ask quietly what you polish so people will see it, a look, a title, a way of seeming busy, a carefully chosen photo, and let one come, not to punish yourself. Name it simply, the way Nanda did: I was vain about this. If something sits under it, a wish to be loved or to feel safe, breathe with it for a moment, without needing to fix it.
Nanda's vanity. The Buddha's half-brother, who once dressed for an audience, opens his song with a plain confession. Today's word.
Your line: I was vain. Nanda's song starts with the trouble and doesn't hide it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Theravada teaching, Nanda's story is told as an example of the Buddha meeting a student where he is, and his verses sit among the Theragatha's songs of the early monks.

chat.says: Why would a monk start his own poem by admitting he was vain?
options: It's honest: his song names the vanity plainly, then thanks the Buddha.
He was boasting; listing his fine robes was meant to impress people.
Every monk had to confess in verse before he could join the order.
chat.meaning: Nanda's verses open plainly: I was given to adornment. Through the Buddha's skillful means he practiced properly and freed his mind.

Theragatha.meaning: the verses of the elder monks

Udana.meaning: a Pali book of short teachings closing with inspired sayings

Sakyan.meaning: of the Sakyas, the Buddha's own clan

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 21.8 (Nanda Sutta: pressed robes, the glazed bowl)
Udana 3.2 (Nanda Sutta: the Sakyan woman, the heaven, the hired hand)

notes: Thag 2.19 (vv. 157–158): confirm the paraphrase: improper attention, attached to adornment (mandana), restless and fickle, oppressed by sensual lust; through the Buddha skilled in means (upayakusala), kinsman of the sun, practiced properly and drew the mind out of becoming.
SN 21.8: confirm pressed/ironed robes, eye ointment, glazed bowl, and the Buddha's advice (forest dweller, almsfood, rag robes, indifferent to sensual pleasures).

Udana 3.2: confirm that Nanda is called the Buddha's brother, son of his mother's sister; the Sakyan girl asking him to return soon; the heaven of the Thirty-three; the promise; monks calling him a hireling; release of the promise. The script softens the text's harsh comparison (a burned she-monkey) to 'no longer compares'.
The hook says Nanda 'made' his song; tradition holds the verses were spoken and memorized, not written.
'Often there's a wish to be loved or safe' in the practice is the writer's gentle suggestion, not a textual claim.
original is null: no single Pali word was chosen; candidates are mandana (adornment) or upaya (means).
Editor: hook reopened as a scene instead of a fragment list (several nearby hooks open with image fragments); cut the 'two lines... two lines' count; varied the practice opener.

Audit: hook said Nanda was 'on his way into town to collect alms' and that 'the Buddha calls him over'; SN 21.8 has Nanda himself approach the Buddha so dressed, with no alms round. Fixed. 'Today, its first word' was inaccurate (the verse opens with ayoniso, careless attention), now 'how it opens'. 'A little comic' about the Udana story changed to 'strange and vivid' (no joke at a text).
